evidence_set: The UK review concluded there was insufficient evidence on whether acute second-hand vaping affects lung function; only 2 small studies at serious risk of bias included second-hand exposure for heart rate or blood pressure, so no conclusion could be drawn. It repeats the Committee on Toxicity's conclusion that vaping is associated with some emissions into ambient air, including nicotine, so that pharmacological effects of nicotine in ambient air may occur in some individuals, and says its own two small studies of short-term second-hand exposure did not allow clear conclusions.

evidence_set: Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

The systematic review's biomarker chapter (60 studies of nicotine, 24 of volatile organic compounds, 28 of tobacco-specific nitrosamines, 9 of other toxicants, 33 of carbon monoxide and 10 of metals; designs, definitions and exposure periods varied and few studies were from the UK). People who vape compared with people who smoke, pooled analyses: nicotine and its breakdown products not significantly different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; volatile organic compound breakdown products mostly significantly lower in 15 analyses (acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower), with formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; nitrosamine breakdown products significantly lower in all 5 analyses (NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower in both analyses; metals mixed. People who vape compared with people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher, as expected (4 analyses); volatile organic compounds not significantly different in the pooled analyses except the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses, which make it difficult to distinguish exposure from vaping from earlier tobacco use, while a randomised trial and a cross-over study suggest levels might fall to those of people who use no nicotine; metals mostly higher; carbon monoxide: no pooled analysis, but some interventional studies of people who switched completely suggested exposure might fall to levels similar to non-use.

The review states that studies used a range of definitions, with some classing people who vape and smoke, vape occasionally or vape daily as one group; that studies with more than one time point mostly explored acute exposure (single use to 7 days) or followed people for 8 days to 12 months, so findings on vaping for more than 12 months could not be summarised; and that few studies could be pooled. Its implications: compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure associated with cigarette smoking, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because comparisons are lacking between people who smoked for many years and have quit and now vape and those who have quit and do not vape, and with people who have never smoked or vaped; past tobacco use can greatly affect many of the biomarkers and most people who vape smoked for many years before; and no difference between people who vape and people who use no nicotine could reflect insensitive measures, background exposure, or relatively similar exposure between people who only vape and people who use no nicotine.

The review concludes that the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, but that based on the toxicant profile in vaping products and aerosols the risk is expected to be much less than that of cigarette smoking (an expectation, not a measured rate). It states that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis; that 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute exposure studies, which cannot answer questions about the cardiovascular health outcomes most relevant to public health; and that studies comparing rates of cardiovascular diseases between non-users, users of tobacco and users of nicotine vaping products are needed. Measured: immediately after use vaping increased heart rate less than smoking; in pooled cross-sectional studies of longer vaping (at least 3 months or one year) people who vaped had lower blood pressure than people who smoked and no difference from people who neither vaped nor smoked; the longest follow-up of arterial stiffness after switching was 4 months.

The Australian review combines an umbrella review of 8 major independent reviews published 2017 to 2021 with a top-up systematic review (searched July 2020, for studies published July 2017 to July 2020), 400 publications in all; the systematic review is registered in PROSPERO and labelled prospective, but its protocol was posted on 31 August 2020, after the search; the top-up studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the evidence graded with GRADE and the National Academies framework. It is based on work commissioned by the Australian Department of Health. It looked at the health effects of e-cigarettes in people and excluded animal, in vitro and biomarker studies as outside its scope, so, on the editors' reading, the biomarker evidence on which the UK review's conclusion on relative harm mainly rests was not counted (the Australian authors note that the UK review focused on comparing e-cigarettes with smoking and on biomarkers).
